activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: The method of loci is a memory trick of linking each part of a text to a place along a familiar route, then walking that route in your mind to recall it.
story:
Carson stood in Grandma Ruth's kitchen with the paper shaking in his hand. In three weeks he would stand in front of the whole congregation and recite the blessing from memory, and right now he could remember exactly one line out of eleven.

"You've walked from my front door to this kitchen a thousand times," Grandma said, sliding a tray of mandelbrot into the oven. "Use that."

"Use walking? That's not a thing."

"It's called the method of loci," she said, tapping her forehead. "Old as Rome, so don't tell me it's not a thing." She refused to say more, which was her way of making him figure it out, and she went back to checking the thermostat, muttering that the oven ran hot and she had to conserve the little patience the machine had left her.

Carson frowned at the paper. Fine. If each line of the blessing lived somewhere along the route, then walking the route in his mind would hand him the lines back, one after another. He tried it right there in the kitchen. The first line went by the crooked mailbox at the front gate, because both felt like a beginning. The second line he set on the porch swing, third on the coat hooks shaped like ducks, and he kept going, hallway, staircase, the doorframe with Grandpa's pencil marks from every birthday. When he reached the eleventh line, he gave it to the sugar bowl on the kitchen table. Then he closed his eyes and walked the whole route without moving his feet, and the whole blessing poured out in order.

His little sister Mira had been watching from the counter, where she'd been building a tower out of cinnamon sticks all afternoon. "Do my spelling words next," she demanded. "I have a bee on Friday and I am going to win it."

"Only if you promise not to be reckless with my route," Carson said. "Don't go moving lines around in my head." He pointed at the sugar bowl. "Line eleven lives there. If you memorize the word 'onomatopoeia' into my sugar bowl, I'm doomed."

"Deal," Mira said, and she screwed her eyes shut and started walking an imaginary hallway, mouthing the first letters of every word. Grandma Ruth pulled the mandelbrot out of the oven, set the tray down, folded her arms, and said, "From the top, Carson. No paper."

He took a breath, thought of the mailbox, and began.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, time goes along the horizontal axis and distance goes up the vertical axis.
story:
Brayden's project sat at the end of table six: a ramp, a marble, and a stopwatch borrowed from his gym teacher. The whole point was to measure how fast the marble rolled by timing it at different distances, then draw a graph. The only problem was his graph, which currently looked like a seagull having a bad day.

"You drew that with your eyes closed, right?" said Priya from the next table, leaning over. She was showing an elastic band car, and the rubber bands kept snapping off and attacking judges.

"I drew it with my eyes open and my brain off," Brayden admitted. He'd marked the seconds going up the side and the distances along the bottom. When he connected his points, the line bent backwards halfway across, as if the marble had rolled uphill, gotten confused, and teleported.

He sat back and remembered science class in the fall, the day Mr. Okoye had made everyone chant it while flapping his arms like a windmill. Brayden had laughed so hard he'd knocked his pencil into the residence of the class hamster, Rocket, who chewed it in half. What had the chant been? Something about the axes. He stared at his ruined seagull. His points made sense as numbers. The line was nonsense. So the numbers weren't the problem; the placement was.

"Wait," he said. He flipped the paper over and started again, writing seconds along the bottom and distance up the side. One, two, three seconds. Twenty centimeters, forty, sixty. He connected the dots and the line climbed steadily, neat and straight. "Time goes along the horizontal axis and distance goes up the vertical axis," he told the graph, feeling slightly like Mr. Okoye. The marble hadn't teleported at all. It had rolled the same speed the whole way, and now the paper proved it.

Priya wandered over with a rubber band stretched between her fingers like a tiny slingshot. "Fixed it?"

"Fixed it. My marble rolls at a steady twenty centimeters per second." He pointed at the slope. "You could mediate an argument between my data points now. They all agree."

Judge Alvarez appeared at the table, clipboard first. He looked at the ramp, then the graph, then Brayden. "Show me," he said, and tapped the stopwatch.

Brayden set the marble at the top of the ramp. "Three," he said, "two, one, release." Priya leaned in so far her rubber band twanged against the table edge.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: In belly breathing, also called diaphragmatic breathing, the belly rises as you breathe in instead of the shoulders lifting, which lets the lungs fill more deeply.
story:
Alexis had failed the last two multiplication quizzes, and tomorrow was the unit test. Her stomach hurt every time she thought about it, and last night she had lain awake until midnight, listening to the furnace tick. She told her friend Priya about it on the bench by the gym.

"It's like my body is stressed even when I'm just sitting there," Alexis said. "I want to figure out what's causing it."

"Maybe it's the test," Priya said. "Obviously."

"No, I mean the stomachache part. I can't see what's making it." Alexis frowned. "My intuition says it's not the food. It happens at the same time every day, right before math."

Priya pulled a crumpled paper from her backpack. It was a handout from the counseling office that had gotten mixed into her folder, titled "Stress Signs and What Helps." Alexis read down the list: tight shoulders, upset stomach, trouble sleeping, racing thoughts. All of it matched.

"Look at this part," Priya said, pointing. "Belly breathing. It's also called diaphragmatic breathing."

The paper said to check whether the belly rises as you breathe in instead of the shoulders lifting, because that lets the lungs fill more deeply. Alexis put one hand on her stomach and one on her shoulder and took a breath. Her shoulder hand moved. Her stomach hand didn't move at all.

"You try," she said. Priya did the same thing, and her shoulder hand rose too.

"So we're both doing it wrong," Priya said. "Which means this is a thing you can actually get wrong. It's a skill."

They practiced through lunch. Alexis breathed in slowly through her nose and watched her hands until the stomach one finally lifted and the shoulder one stayed still. The tight feeling in her chest loosened a little. She tried it four more times to make sure it wasn't a fluke, and each time the belly rose first.

That night she followed the second half of the handout, a sleep routine: same time every night, no screens, backpack packed before bed. She did three slow belly breaths with her hand on her stomach, and she was asleep before she could count the furnace ticks.

The next morning, her stomach was quiet. She took the test, and when she got to problem nine she felt her shoulders creep up toward her ears. She set her pencil down, put a hand on her belly, and breathed until she felt it rise.

After class, Mr. Roark handed back the quizzes. "Alexis, see me a second."

She stayed, expecting the worst, imagining her grade decomposing into a pile of missing assignments. He turned her paper over. Problem nine, the one she had breathed through, was the only one marked wrong.

"That's the twist," Priya said later, laughing. "You got a ninety-four, and the one you missed was the one you relaxed on."

"That's not the twist," Alexis said. "The twist is my stomach didn't hurt at all."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The Canadian Charter applies to governments and their actions, not directly to private businesses or individuals.
story:
Hannah spread her homework across Grandpa's kitchen table: a photocopied page of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and a blank sheet for her explanation of one right. She had picked Section 8, protection against unreasonable search, because it sounded dramatic. Grandpa set down two mugs of tea and pulled a chair around beside her instead of across the table.

She read the section out loud twice, then wrote her first sentence: "This means nobody can ever search you." Grandpa tapped the page. "Read it again. Which word are you skipping?" She found it: "unreasonable." Her teacher wanted them to explain a right in their own words, and hers had quietly changed the rule.

The memory came back to her then, from last fall. She had marched into a convenience store with her backpack and the owner had pointed at a sign that said NO BACKPACKS. She had said, "That's against the Charter. I have rights." The owner had just looked at her, and her friend Priya had dragged her outside before it turned into a real argument. At the time she had decided the owner simply didn't know the law.

She pulled out her phone and searched for "Charter who does it apply to." The results were consistent. She read one line, then another, frowning. "Grandpa," she said, "it says the Charter applies to governments and their actions. Not to private businesses or individuals. Not directly."

"So was the store owner breaking the Charter when he banned backpacks?"

"No," Hannah said slowly. "No, he wasn't. That's a different kind of rule, like a store policy. I was wrong." She sat back. "Priya's going to hear about this." Then she thought of a way to test it, because it seemed too strange to accept from one search. She imagined the same sign posted at the public library, run by the city. The sign at the store was a policy; a government doing something similar would touch the Charter. It was a logical distinction, and once she saw it, the whole thing held together.

She rewrote her sentence: "The Charter puts limits on what governments can do, so a rule that's fine for a private store might not be fine for a public one." She underlined it. Then she turned to Grandpa. "You knew the whole time, didn't you? At the library last month, when I complained about the backpack thing." He raised his mug. "The Charter keeps a certain hierarchy in place," he said. "I wanted you to demonstrate you could climb it yourself." She took her tea out to the porch and texted Priya: "I owe the store an apology."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: To finish 800 metres in three minutes on a 400-metre track, a runner must average 90 seconds for each lap.
story:
Simon crouched behind the start line at the far end of the field, flipping his race number over in his hands. Coach Reyes had said the words once, in the gym, and walked away: "Three minutes if you want the record." Simon had no idea what that meant for his legs.

He found a pencil stub in his sock, the one he kept for math class, and wrote on the back of the number. Three minutes for eight hundred metres. He chewed the pencil. Then he remembered the chalk line Coach had pointed at on the track, halfway around, and the way she had counted the curved sections out loud last week. The track was four hundred metres all the way around. He stopped chewing. Four hundred went into eight hundred twice, so if the whole race took three minutes, then each lap had to take half of that. Ninety seconds. He wrote "90" in big numbers and underlined it twice.

Last spring flashed back at him, sharp as a starter's gun. The district meet, his first eight hundred. He had sprinted the first lap like it was a hundred, arms pumping, passing everybody, feeling like a king. Then his legs had turned to rope in the second lap and four runners had gone past him before the finish. He had stood with his hands on his knees and watched their backs. His problem had never been speed. It had been something he couldn't see, hiding in the way he spent his legs too early.

"Simon, heat two," called the timer, a kid from the affluent side of town whose parents bought the team all its stopwatches. "You're the only consumer of lane one today, so enjoy it."

"Whistle me the ninety," Simon said. "First lap."

The kid frowned. "You want me to yell at ninety seconds?"

"Just do it."

The gun cracked. Simon counted his steps and held back, even when Darrell from Jefferson surged ahead. Sixty, seventy, the pack stringing out, his chest telling him to go, go. Then the whistle: "Ninety!" Simon crossed the line right on it, Darrell three seconds up, and Simon smiled, because Darrell was already breathing like a punctured tire.

Simon did not cease moving, did not sprint yet, just lifted his knees a little more. By the final curve the gap had shrunk to a stride. Simon heard Darrell's ragged breath beside him, felt the number flapping against his chest with "90" pressed to his skin, and drove for the line.

"Two fifty-eight," the timer shouted, thumb on the watch. "Who taught you that?"

Simon turned the number over so the pencil side showed. "Nobody," he said. "I did the math."

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: The brain keeps developing until about age 25, which makes young people more vulnerable to nicotine addiction than adults.
story:
Simon sat in the dentist's waiting room with a poster rolled under his arm and a note card balanced on his knee. Tomorrow he had to explain to his class how nicotine hooks the brain, and his plan so far consisted of the words "reward pathway" written at the top of the card and a drawing of a brain wearing a fishing hat. "You look like a man about to resign from school entirely," said Marisol, dropping into the chair beside him with a magazine she had no intention of reading.

"It's invisible," Simon said. "That's the problem. I can't show them a molecule walking into a brain and flipping a switch." He tapped the card. "Nicotine gets in, and the brain releases dopamine, this feel-good chemical, in the reward pathway. The brain notices, decides it likes nicotine, and starts demanding more. But nobody can see any of that happen. I need proof you can't see." Marisol flipped a page. "Then prove it the way my brother proved the dog was stealing socks. He couldn't see it either. He set up a camera, kind of, and then a trap with a sock and a door."

Simon thought about that all through his cleaning, even with the hygienist poking around like a scavenger hunting for one last popcorn kernel. His idea formed somewhere between the flossing and the rinse. A hidden cause still leaves a pattern, and you can test a pattern. He would draw two brains on his poster and show what repeated nicotine did to the pathway over time, then show what happened when the nicotine stopped. If the demands got louder before they faded, that was the invisible hook leaving a visible mark.

In the parking lot afterward, Marisol's cousin Devon was leaning against the fence, and he held out a small pen-shaped thing with a grin. "One hit," he said. "It's watermelon. Barely even counts." Simon looked at it, then at his poster tube. "Nope," he said. "The brain keeps developing until about age 25. That makes teenagers more vulnerable to nicotine addiction than adults." Devon blinked. "So my brain is literally still under construction, and you want to pour nicotine on the construction site?" Marisol snorted. "He's been rehearsing all afternoon. It's kind of subjective whether that was for you or for his presentation."

"It was for both," Simon said. "Consider it a free preview." Devon pocketed the vape with theatrical sadness and muttered something about nerds with posters. Simon unrolled the poster on the hood of his mom's car, spread it flat with both hands, and held up his marker. "Now help me draw a brain in a hard hat."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: Galileo studied motion by rolling balls down gentle ramps, which slowed the motion enough for him to time it.
story:
Emily's problem was simple: the ball rolled across the lab table so fast that nobody could time it, and the graph she was supposed to draw had exactly three sad dots on it, all clumped at the far end.

"It's over before I even click the stopwatch," said Marcus, her lab partner, clicking the stopwatch anyway.

Emily looked at the blank grid on her worksheet. To draw a distance-time graph, they needed to quantify how far the ball went in a measured time, several times, at marks along the way. That was the whole assignment. She glared at the ball, which sat at the end of the table looking innocent, like a small round organism that had evolved specifically to ruin her grade.

Then she remembered the field trip in October. At the science museum there had been a long, gentle ramp with a ball you could release yourself, and a plaque she'd only half read while waiting for her turn. She'd thought it was just a slow, boring version of a slide. But the ball on that ramp had crept down so gradually that even the kid behind her, who spent the whole visit dropping his juice, could have timed it. The plaque had said something about a man named Galileo. She closed her eyes and pulled the words back up: Galileo studied motion by rolling balls down gentle ramps, which slowed the motion enough for him to time it.

"Get the board," she said.

They propped one end of the whiteboard on a stack of three textbooks, making a shallow slope, and let the ball roll down its smooth back. Now they could time it. At twenty centimeters, their stopwatch said one point four seconds. At forty, two point seven. At sixty, four point two. Marcus called out numbers; Emily plotted them, and the dots fell into a line so straight she checked twice to make sure she hadn't drawn it with her ruler by accident. The line climbed steadily upward. Speed, drawn from nothing but distance and time, was suddenly sitting on her paper.

Mr. Okafor stopped at their table and picked up the worksheet. "Nice line. Where'd the ramp idea come from?"

"A dead guy," Emily said. "Kind of obsolete, but his ramp worked."

He handed it back, and his eye drifted to the corner where a motion sensor sat plugged in, the one that had been broken since September. He jiggled its cord, and the little green light flickered on.

"You could have just used this," he said.

Marcus looked at the stopwatch, then at the sensor, then at their beautiful hand-drawn line. "We like the ramp," he said, and set the ball rolling again.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: Japji Sahib is also recited at the Sikh Khalsa initiation ceremony, called Amrit Sanchar.
story:
The bunting over the festival stage had snapped loose on one side, and every time the wind lifted, the whole banner flapped like a luminous orange fish trying to escape. Marcus watched it while his grandmother steered him by the elbow toward the langar tent, where the smell of cardamom and fried dough made his stomach growl loudly enough that two aunties laughed.

"You have to know it by Sunday," she said. "All of it. Not mostly it."

"I know, Bebe. Mostly is almost all."

"Almost is not all." She set down her plate. "Your uncle will be there. He will listen."

Marcus groaned. Japji Sahib was long, and the Punjabi words slipped out of his memory the way water slipped off a duck. He had been repeating it for two weeks, in the shower, on the bus, once out loud in math class until Priya Nair leaned over and whispered, "Buddy, you're chanting." He could not figure out why it had to be word-for-word perfect when nobody was even testing him on the meaning yet.

He found his cousin Simran near the kite stall, arguing with a kid about whether a kite was technically an organism. "It eats wind," the kid insisted. "It breathes."

"It has no cells," Simran said. "Case closed. Marcus, tell him."

"It has no cells," Marcus agreed, then slumped onto a hay bale. "Simran, why does Bebe want Japji Sahib exactly right? It's just my Sunday thing."

Simran snorted. "Sunday thing? Uncle Harjit is taking Amrit. At the Khalsa initiation ceremony. It's called Amrit Sanchar. And Japji Sahib is recited there too." She picked up the kite string. "So when you say it at home, and he says it there, you're saying the same thing at the same time. Sort of."

Marcus sat up. Same words, same morning, two places. That was the point. It was not a test of his memory. It was a rope you held from your end while someone else held the other. He tested it right there, closing his eyes and reciting the first verse, and when he stumbled on the fourth line, he felt the wobble like a dropped stitch.

"Simran," he said, opening one eye, "if I mess up on Sunday, does Uncle feel it?"

"He'll console you with jalebi, probably."

Marcus grinned and started the verse again, slower, letting each word land like a foot on a narrow bridge.

"Better," Simran said. "Now say the next one."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Simmering a sauce with the lid off lets water escape as steam, so the sauce slowly gets thicker.
story:
Simon stood at the counter with an onion, a chef's knife, and a plan. Tonight was his turn to cook, and Mom had left one note on the fridge: "Sauce from scratch. Dad's home at 6:30 sharp." It was 5:40. The onion glared at him like it knew he was afraid of it.

He curled his fingers into a claw, knuckles forward, fingertips tucked safely back, exactly the way the cooking video had shown. The knife tip stayed on the cutting board while the blade rocked through the onion in even slices. His eyes streamed anyway, and he pretended they were tears of respect. "You fought well," he told the onion, sweeping the pieces into the hot pan. They hissed and softened, and Simon felt like a wizard.

He crushed the canned tomatoes in with his hands, which was the best part of the entire evening, added salt and a pinch of sugar, and clapped the lid on the pot. Then he sat back and waited for greatness. He checked the clock at 6:05, at 6:15, and finally at 6:25, when his little sister Maya wandered in and leaned over the pot.

"Why is it soup?" she asked.

"It's not soup. It's sauce."

She dipped a spoon in, let it drip, and raised an eyebrow at the long watery trail. "Dad hates watery sauce. He calls it pasta bathwater. Remember the Great Bathwater Incident?"

Simon remembered. Dad had been dramatic about it for a week. Simon lifted the lid and stared into the red, sloshy pot, thinking hard. Steam had been building up under that lid the whole time, all pearly and dripping back down. Where did water go when you boiled the kettle? Out the top, as vapor, and gone. But the lid had been trapping it, sending it right back into the pot like a boomerang. If he wanted the sauce thicker, he had to let the water eliminate itself, escape into the air and never come back.

"Maya, grab a spoon and be my taster," he said, sliding the lid off completely and turning the heat to a steady simmer. The sauce began to bubble, and little wisps of vapor curled up and vanished. Every minute, more water left and more sauce stayed behind. Maya stationed herself on a stool like a judge at a baking show.

At 6:28, they tested it. The spoon came out coated, the sauce clinging thick and slow. Maya nodded gravely. "Bathwater status eliminated."

Car headlights swept the kitchen wall at exactly 6:30. Dad walked in, sniffed, and peered into the pot. Simon held his breath while Dad twirled a forkful of pasta through the sauce, watching it cling instead of puddle.

"Well?" Simon asked.

Dad looked at Maya, who looked at Simon, who looked at the pot with enormous dignity.

"The vote is unanimous," Dad announced, already reaching for a second helping. "No bathwater in this house tonight."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version of the periodic table in 1869.
story:
Aubrey spread the printed periodic table across the kitchen table and glared at it like it had insulted her. Tomorrow's quiz would ask her to find the number of protons in an element, and she could not make sense of the little numbers at all. Gold had a 79 somewhere near its name, and iron had a 26, and she could not tell which number meant protons, which meant something else, and which one she was supposed to hunt down like a scavenger digging through a junk drawer.

Her little brother Theo wandered in holding a postcard from their class trip to the science museum, which had happened two weeks before Aubrey got sick and missed it. He slid it across the table. On the front was a photograph of an old handwritten chart, faded and crowded. "That's from the timeline wall," he said. "The Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version of the periodic table in 1869. I copied it off the plaque because it looked like a cool cheat sheet."

Aubrey frowned at the postcard. The old table looked nothing like the neat colored grid in front of her. Some squares were empty, as if Mendeleev had simply left room for elements nobody had found yet. She flipped the postcard over and found a message she had written to herself the morning of the field trip, before she knew she would be home with a fever instead: "Dear Aubrey, sit in the front for the chemistry exhibit. Take notes. You will thank yourself during the quiz." She had never gotten the chance. Her stomach did a small, sour flip, and she decided she would invest the whole evening in figuring this out on her own, postcard and all.

She started with the one thing she remembered from before she got sick: the atomic number. She traced her finger down the grid, hunting for the pattern. Hydrogen, number 1. Helium, number 2. Lithium, number 3. She tested an idea against iron. If the big number, 26, was the atomic number, and if the atomic number counted protons, then iron should have 26 protons. She checked gold, at 79, and oxygen, at 8, and the rule held every single time, like a lock accepting one key. The atomic number was the proton count. That was the whole secret, and nobody had needed to tell her.

"Twenty-six," she said out loud, tapping iron. "Iron has twenty-six protons." Theo, who was dunking a cookie in his milk, looked up. "That's it? That's the hard thing?" She threw a folded napkin at him, but she was grinning.

There was still a cost, and she knew it. She had missed the museum, the front row, the exhibit where a docent let kids hold a sample of real gold, and no amount of kitchen-table work would give that day back. But she pulled a blank index card toward her and wrote "Au, 79" in careful letters, then "Fe, 26" beneath it, building her own small timeline from Mendeleev's ghost of a table to this one. She pinned the postcard above her desk, message side out. "Dear future Aubrey," she said to the empty room, and uncapped her pen.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In Richard Connell's 1924 story The Most Dangerous Game, the island's name, Ship-Trap Island, and sailors' fear of it hint at the danger waiting there.
story:
Sofia spread the photocopy across the library table and read the first page of "The Most Dangerous Game" for the third time. Her English teacher had written one comment on her last essay: "Claims need evidence from the text." Sofia wanted to fix that before Friday, and she had picked this story because everyone in class said it was full of tricks hiding in plain sight.

At the next table, a boy named Marcus was building something out of straws and tape, a model sailboat for his science project. He kept glancing over at her pages. "Are you reading that hunting story?" he asked. "My brother read it last year. He wouldn't tell me the ending. He said it was too good to spoil."

"I can't even get past the beginning," Sofia said. "The two guys are on a yacht, talking in the dark, and one of them mentions an island." She tapped the page. "Rainsford says the sailors call it Ship-Trap Island. And the old guy Whitney says the place has a reputation, that the crew feels a chill about it, like something evil is there."

"So it's a spooky island. Big deal."

"That's what I thought the first time. But my teacher wants foreshadowing, clues about what's coming, and a symbol too. And this name feels like a clue." She pulled out a fresh index card and wrote on it. Marcus leaned over his rudder, which he had bent trying to make it turn, and watched her.

"Think about it," she said, testing the idea out loud. "The characters just sail past and talk about it. But the author picked that name on purpose. A ship-trap is a thing that catches ships. Sailors being afraid of it means something bad already happened there or will. The name is doing work." She underlined the sentence twice. "So when the story later ends up on that island, whatever happens there was set up from page one. That's the evidence."

"Can you use my boat as your symbol?" Marcus said, holding up the sailboat with its crooked rudder. "I need someone to look at this thing and tell me if it says 'genius' or 'kind of sad.'"

Sofia laughed and took the boat. She turned it in her hands. "It says you tried, which is more than my essay did." Then she stopped. "Actually, that's it. The yacht is a symbol. These men are safe and comfortable, in control, like the boat's rudder steers it wherever it wants. If danger comes from an island that traps ships, then everything that makes them feel safe is about to be taken away." She set the boat down carefully and wrote two more lines on her card, pressing hard so the words would show.

Marcus pried the rudder off with his thumbnail and started reshaping it. "So my boat is a symbol of lost safety?"

"My teacher would say don't push it," Sofia said, and slid her card to the corner of the table where she could see it, the underlined sentence faceup.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: SUM skips cells that hold text, so a number stored as text is silently left out of the total.
story:
Clara needed the spreadsheet finished by the end of lunch period, because the class was voting on a new pet for the science room and Mr. Ruiz wanted the totals charted before fifth period. She had typed every vote into a column, forty-two numbers in all, and then written the formula Ms. Okafor had shown them: =SUM(B2:B43). She pressed Enter, and the total came out 38. Clara counted her paper ballots again. Forty-two. She counted twice.

Her friend Devon leaned over from the next computer. "Mine's wrong too. I have 37." He had also pasted his numbers in from the shared file the class had built on the whiteboard screen yesterday. Clara looked down her column. All the cells held digits as far as she could see. Then she clicked on B17, which should have been Marcus's ballot. In the formula bar at the top, instead of 3 it said '3, with a straight apostrophe sitting in front of the number like a splinter. She clicked on B2, which she had typed herself. No apostrophe. She checked a few more. Most were clean, but B17, B24 and B40 all had the apostrophe, and all three had been pasted from the shared file.

"Those came from the paste," Clara said. "Three cells. Forty-two minus three is 39, but my total says 38." She counted the pasted rows again and found a fourth, B31, hiding near the bottom. Four cells. She retested her idea by typing 5 into a fresh cell, typing '5 into the cell below it, and summing only those two. The answer came out 5, not 10. So SUM skipped cells that held text, and a number stored as text was left out of the total, quietly, without any error message. "It doesn't break," she told Devon. "It just leaves the text ones out." He groaned and resigned himself to checking all forty of his rows one at a time.

Clara retyped the four numbers by hand, deleting the apostrophe in the formula bar each time. She pressed Enter on the SUM again. 42. Then she highlighted the vote column, clicked the chart button, chose bars, and the bar chart appeared: hamsters 14, fish 11, gecko 9, hermit crabs 8. She stretched the chart across the bottom of the sheet and added a title. Devon, two rows over, was still clicking through his column, muttering.

Ms. Okafor stopped behind Clara's screen on her way past. "Nice chart. Why were you retyping those cells?"

"Because they were pasted as text," Clara said. "A number stored as text gets skipped by SUM."

Ms. Okafor looked at the chart, then at the column, then gave a small nod and moved on. Clara printed her sheet and pinned it to the board beside the ballot box, where the class would see the bars before the bell.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A Torah scroll is written without vowels or musical marks, so a bar or bat mitzvah student learns the chanted melody of their reading in advance from a printed book.
story:
Eve sat at the kitchen table with her practice book open to page forty-seven. In three weeks she would read from the Torah scroll for her bat mitzvah, and every line in the book was covered with little symbols. Some marks told her which vowel to sing, and some curled above the letters like tiny staircases, telling her the melody, up or down, held long or short. She had been memorizing her portion for two months, and she still stumbled in the same three places.

"You're mouthing it again," her brother Danny said from the counter, where he was stealing grapes. "Gross."

"I'm practicing. Some of us have a ceremony to prepare for."

"Only a small percentage of people mouth words at the kitchen table," he said, and she threw a crumpled napkin at him.

That Thursday was the rehearsal at the synagogue. The rabbi's assistant, a college student named Orli, unlocked the ark and rolled the great scroll open on the reading table while Eve stood beside it holding her book. "Find your portion," Orli said. "Start wherever you're comfortable."

Eve ran her finger along the columns and stopped. Then she looked closer. Her stomach dropped. The parchment had letters, but nothing else. No vowels. No melodic marks. Just bare consonants, row after row, like a fence with the spaces between the pickets blacked out.

"Where's the rest of it?" she asked.

"That's all of it," Orli said. She didn't say anything more, just watched, as if waiting.

Eve's mind went fast. The scroll was the real thing, the one they read from every week, so this was how it always looked. Which meant everyone who read Torah, the rabbi, the old man with the walker, her cousin last spring, had chanted melody that was not printed on the page. She thought of her practice book with its marks. That was where the tune lived. Everyone learned it there first, in advance, and carried it in their memory to the blank scroll.

"So the book gives me the melody," Eve said slowly, "and I'm supposed to already have it in my head when I stand here."

"Stand here and try," Orli said.

Eve put her finger on the first word of her portion. The shapes looked naked without their marks, but she made herself hum the phrase before she sang it. The melody rose where the little staircase had risen. It dropped where she remembered it dropping. Her voice wavered on the second verse and she stopped, laughed once, and started the verse over. When she finished the passage, Orli nodded.

"I'm going to run through it ten more times tonight," Eve said. "Without looking at the marks."

"Nine," Orli said. "You're already at ten on the ones you know." She rolled the scroll closed and pointed at the practice book still lying open on the table. "And this one, you can close."

Eve closed it and put it in her backpack. On her way out she said, "Danny is never going to believe the scroll is blank."

"Blank and holy," Orli said, locking the ark. "Now go home and chant to your brother. Infectious, that kind of thing."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Checking in privately afterward with a classmate who was teased, and telling them it was not okay, can help them feel less alone even if nobody stepped in at the time.
story:
The sprinklers had started just as the piñata came down, and by the time Victoria ducked under the canopy, the smell of wet grass had begun to saturate the whole backyard. Jonah's thirteenth birthday, twenty kids, a table of cake nobody was eating yet. Someone had put on music. It should have been easy.

Then Dylan grabbed Noah's backpack and held it over his head. "Look, he brought his rock collection. To a party." A few kids laughed. Noah reached up, missed, went red. Victoria stood ten feet away with a cup of punch and did nothing. She told herself the joke would burn out, that jumping in would make it a bigger deal, that a real diplomat would know when to stay quiet. Dylan dropped the backpack in the mud, and the laughing faded on its own, and everyone drifted toward the cake table. Noah picked up his bag alone.

Victoria carried her punch around for twenty minutes, watching Noah sit at the far end of the canopy with his ruined backpack, wiping mud off a rock with his thumb. She kept drafting lines in her head. If she said something loud, Dylan would come back with something worse. If she said nothing, she was just another kid who laughed, even though she hadn't laughed. What she couldn't see was whether her silence, later, could be fixed, or whether it was already set like concrete. She decided to run a small test. One sentence, quiet, just to him, and she'd watch his face.

She crossed the wet grass and sat on the bench beside him. "That wasn't okay," she said. "What Dylan did." Noah kept polishing the rock. "You don't have to say anything," she added. "I just wanted you to know I thought it was wrong."

He turned the rock over. It was exceptional, a chunk of quartz with a vein of purple running through it. "This one's amethyst," he said. "Found it behind the soccer field." He held it out so she could see. "Nobody said anything," he said after a minute. "When it happened." Victoria's face went hot. "I know. I froze. I'm sorry." Noah set the rock on the bench between them, closer to her than to him, and started pulling granola bars out of the muddy backpack, stacking the dry ones in a neat little pile.

The canopy dripped. Victoria helped him stack. Behind them, Dylan's voice rose over the music, complaining that his sneakers were soaked and that the party was, in his expert opinion, the worst one all year. He stood alone at the cake table, and not one person came over to agree with him.

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: Two things happening together, a correlation, does not prove that one causes the other; a third factor may cause both.
story:
Noemie sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with a stack of index cards, a pencil, and a debate packet that was due in five days. The motion was "Schools should ban junk food," and she had to build a whole case with a claim, evidence, and a warrant for every single point. Her grandmother slid a mug of cocoa next to the cards and said the cards were the most organized thing she'd seen in that kitchen since 1987.

"You need a claim," Noemie said, writing at the top of the first card. "Then evidence, then the warrant, which is the bridge between them." She was talking mostly to the teapot, which was the only thing in the room that seemed to be listening. Her grandmother was humming and arranging peppers on a baking sheet. Noemie formulated her first claim: "Junk food makes students unhealthy." Easy. Evidence would be studies, statistics, something official. The warrant, though, was where she got stuck, because her older brother Theo kept sending her useless facts by text.

Theo burst through the back door with sand on his shoes and a popsicle in his hand. "Did you know," he said, dropping into the chair across from her, "that ice cream and sunburn go up at exactly the same time in summer? Ice cream causes sunburn. I'm going to use that at the dinner table tonight." He grinned like he'd won something.

Noemie looked at him, then at her cards, then at him again. "That's not how it works. The ice cream doesn't do anything to your skin." She pulled out a fresh card and drew two rising arrows side by side. "They go up together, but that's just a correlation. Two things happening together doesn't prove that one causes the other." Theo chewed his popsicle stick and squinted at her arrows. "Then why do they both go up?"

Noemie tapped her pencil, testing her own idea before she said it out loud. "Something else makes them both rise. A third thing." She drew a sun in the corner of the card and an arrow from the sun down to each of the other two arrows. "Summer does both. Sunscreen, picnic tables, everything at once." Theo slumped. "So I can't blame dessert for my sunburn." "You could try," Noemie said, "but Grandma will formulate a counterargument in about four seconds."

She turned back to her case with new energy. The tedious part, she had thought, would be finding statistics. Now she saw the real trap: her second card claimed that schools with junk food vending machines had lower test scores, and her evidence was a single bar graph from a website with clip art in the header. She stared at it. The schools with vending machines were also the biggest schools, in the hottest towns, with the least funding. Something else might be pulling both numbers down at once, some third component she hadn't even named yet. She crossed out the card, flipped it over, and wrote on the back, "Find the third arrow."

At dinner, Theo set down his fork and announced, "Ice cream does not cause sunburn, because correlation does not imply causation." Noemie raised her cocoa mug like a trophy, and her grandmother, without looking up from the peppers, said, "Then who ate the last of my ice cream, since clearly nobody here can prove it?"

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: A pivot table treats 'Gr 7' and 'Grade 7' as two separate groups, so answers must be typed consistently before they are summarised.
story:
Sydney had promised the student council she would have the survey results summarized by Sunday night, and now it was Saturday afternoon, and the spreadsheet on Priya's laptop just sat there blinking at her. Three hundred students had answered the question "Should we get a second vending machine?", and Sydney's whole plan revolved around making sense of their answers by grade, so the council could see exactly who wanted what. Priya's mom had offered the kitchen table, lemonade, and the warning that they had better not spill anything because of the mortgage and the general state of the family finances, and then she had retreated to the garden.

"Okay," Priya said, leaning over Sydney's shoulder. "You put your answers in rows, and then you drag the grade column over here, and the program counts everything for you. It's called a pivot table." Sydney dragged, clicked, and a summary appeared. Grade 6: 94 votes. Grade 8: 88 votes. Grade 7: 51 votes. Grade 7: 63 votes.

Sydney stared at the screen. "Grade seven appears twice."

"That's impossible. There's one grade seven." Priya grabbed a cookie and chewed at the problem sideways. Sydney scrolled through the raw answers, and there it was: some students had typed "Gr 7" and others had typed "Grade 7." She felt a small, satisfying click in her head, the kind that came when a hidden rule revealed itself. "The computer doesn't know those are the same thing," she said. "It thinks they're two different groups, so it split them up."

"So half the seventh graders are hiding in the wrong drawer," Priya said. "Like socks."

Fixing it was worse than finding it. Sydney had to go through a hundred and fourteen rows one by one, changing "Gr 7" to "Grade 7," while Priya read them out loud in a robot voice until Sydney threatened her with the lemonade pitcher. By the time they finished, her eyes ached and the afternoon was gone; Priya's brother had eaten the rest of the cookies and their plan to watch a movie had quietly died. But when Sydney dragged the grade column across again, the summary came out clean: Grade 6, 94. Grade 7, 114. Grade 8, 88. Two hundred ninety-six students, and the seventh graders were overwhelmingly in favor of the vending machine.

"It's plausible that the seventh graders just really want snacks," Priya said, reading the numbers upside down. Sydney saved the file twice, then emailed it to the council, then sat back and looked at the crumbs on the plate where the cookies used to be.

"Worth it," she said. "Next time, though, we bring backup cookies."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Earth's axis points in the same direction in space all year, so for part of the orbit the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun and later leans away.
story:
Eva dragged the floor lamp out the back door, set her brother's globe on the picnic table, and pointed at the fence. "See that gray patch on the wood? That's lichen. If lichen can grow on our dumb fence for a hundred years, I can learn one science thing by tomorrow."

"Deep," said Marcus, holding her mom's phone like a movie camera. "Take it from the top."

Eva stood the lamp in the middle of the yard and clicked it on. The bulb was her sun. The globe was Earth. Tomorrow she had to explain the seasons to her whole class, and Ms. Okafor had said the presentations had to demonstrate something, not just talk about it. Eva wanted the demonstration to be the best one, and she had one afternoon.

"Okay. Earth goes around the sun like this." She walked the globe in a slow circle around the lamp. "And the axis is tilted, so watch the top half, the Northern Hemisphere. When it leans toward the sun, boom, summer." She stopped and squinted. Something was wrong. The top of the globe was leaning away, not toward. She frowned and turned the globe in her hands until the north leaned at the bulb again, then kept walking, and by the time she reached the far side of her orbit she had rotated the whole thing without noticing. Now north leaned away again. It contradicted everything she'd written on her notecards.

"No, no, no." She checked the notecard. It said seasons happen because Earth's axis points in the same direction in space all year. Same direction. All year. She read it twice, then looked at the globe, then at the fence, because pacing helped her think.

"Marcus. Hold my shoulders so I face the shed."

"Why?"

"Because I'm Earth. You're space." He grabbed her shoulders, giggling, and she tilted sideways like a leaning tower, top half drooping toward the lamp. She walked one full circle around the light. When she got back to where she started, her tilted self faced the shed again, leaning the same way she had at the beginning. Halfway around, the lamp lit her top half full on. On the other side, her top leaned away and the light fell soft and slanted on her.

"That's it!" she shouted. "The axis points the same direction the whole time. That's why the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the sun for part of the orbit, and leans away later. I kept turning the globe. I was ruining my own planet!"

"So stop turning it," Marcus said.

She made him do it with her, both of them walking the globe around the lamp, shoulders squared to the shed, counting out loud. Six laps. Not one accidental turn. Marcus had promised to be her camera stand as a voluntary act of kindness, though he kept calling it blackmail, since she'd agreed to do his dishes for a week.

"Final take," Eva said, lifting the globe. "Rolling."

The lamp blazed, the fence lichen watched from the sidelines, and Eva stepped into her orbit, north pole tilted steady, holding steady, holding steady, all the way around the light.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: In written dialogue, a new paragraph begins each time a different character starts speaking, so readers can tell who is talking.
story:
Livia spread her notebook across the cafe table and stabbed her pencil at the page. Her story had everything she wanted: a storm, a lighthouse, a sinister shadow moving along the cliff. But when her friend Marcus slid into the other chair and grabbed the notebook, his face went blank after two paragraphs.

"Who's talking here?" Marcus asked. "The keeper or the girl? They both say stuff in this big blob and I can't tell."

"Read it again," Livia said. "It's obvious."

He read it again. "No. Seriously. I'm lost." He tapped the block of back-and-forth lines. "The keeper says 'the light is failing,' then someone says 'I'll climb the tower,' then someone says 'don't.' Who's who?"

Livia took the notebook back and squinted at it. He was right. She had squeezed four speeches into one paragraph, and on the page they had melted together like the steam rising off his hot chocolate. She had calibrated the plot carefully, timed the storm to hit at exactly the right moment, but the words themselves were a mess.

She flipped to a printed story she kept in her bag, one she'd read three times already, and laid it beside her draft. Her eyes moved down the published page. Every time a new character started to speak, a new paragraph began. She checked the next conversation. Same thing. Every single speech by a different speaker got its own paragraph. That was the logic of it, she realized, a system underneath the page she'd never noticed, like studs inside a wall.

"Give me a minute," she said. She drew a line before each speech in her draft, then rewrote them, splitting the blob apart. The keeper's warning sat alone in its paragraph. The girl's answer sat in the next one. "Now read."

Marcus leaned in. His finger tracked down the page. "Okay, okay, the keeper first, then her, then him. I can see it now. Nobody has to tell me." He kept reading, and his finger moved faster. At the tower scene he looked up. "Wait, she drops the match? Livia, you can't leave it there."

"That's the climax. The whole story points at that moment."

"Then what happens?"

Livia picked up her pencil. "I don't know yet. Ask me in twenty minutes."

Marcus dragged his chair around to her side of the table. "Then I'm staying for the ending."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: The climax is the turning point of a story, the moment of highest tension when the main conflict is decided one way or the other.
story:
Aria tapped her pencil against the kitchen table and stared at the mess of highlighted paragraphs on her laptop screen. The assignment was due Friday: a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax, and the winner would be read aloud at the district writing festival, which everyone agreed was the most prestigious contest their school entered. Her draft had dialogue. What it did not have, according to her friend Marcus, was a climax in the right place.

His message sat in the group chat, waiting: "The climax is the robbery scene. It has to be. Everything else is just people talking." Aria reread her own story, hunting for the moment she had felt sure was her climax, the scene where Nadia finally opens the locked box and finds her grandmother's medal. She had put quotation marks around every line of dialogue, commas inside them, she had checked twice, but now she could not tell which scene was the peak and which was just noise.

She typed back: "I thought the box scene was the climax." Marcus answered with a shrug emoji, which helped exactly nothing. Their third group member, Priya, was offline, and the laptop emitted a soft chime as another message from Marcus appeared: "The robbery decides everything, though. That's the point."

Aria pushed the computer aside and thought about her own grandmother's jewelry box, the one on the shelf in the hall. Nobody could see what was inside it. What made you lean toward it, what made your hand hover, was knowing that opening it would settle something, one way or the other. She pulled the computer back and looked at her story again with that idea in her head. The robbery, she realized, did not decide anything. Nadia lost the box in the robbery, yes, but the story could have ended there with either outcome and nothing would have changed. The moment everything got decided, the moment the whole conflict turned, was later, when Nadia opened the box and had to choose whether to tell the truth about how she got it back.

She typed into the chat: "The climax is the turning point of the story, the moment of highest tension when the main conflict gets decided one way or the other." Then she added, "The robbery raises the tension. The box scene decides it. That's the difference." Her hands were shaking a little, the way they did when she argued with Marcus and actually meant it.

For a long minute the chat was silent. Then Priya's name lit up at the top of the screen, back from dinner, and three dots appeared and vanished twice before her reply came through: "She's right, Marcus. Read the last page again. Everything after the box scene is falling action."

Marcus sent one more message: "Fine. But fix your punctuation in scene two. You put the period outside the quotes."

Aria grinned, deleted the stray period, and dragged the robbery scene three paragraphs earlier.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: The Koppen climate classification, still used on climate maps today, was developed by Wladimir Koppen, a climatologist born in Russia who worked in Germany.
story:
Emile slid two graph sheets across the library table and frowned at them like they had insulted him. His report was due Monday, and he had picked deserts and rainforests because they sounded easy, but the graphs said otherwise. The desert line stayed low and flat for rainfall all year, while the rainforest line climbed so high in some months that it ran off the top of the graph. He had drawn the rainforest bars so tall that his ruler tore the paper. He wanted this to be the best report in Mr. Alvarez's class, better than Priya's, and right now it looked like a mess of ink and torn edges.

Then he noticed the climate map pinned above the atlas shelf. Tiny letters were printed in each region: Af across the Amazon, BWh across the Sahara. He copied them onto his torn sheet and typed them into the library computer, though the notice said he was only authorized to use the research terminals for homework, which this technically was, so he decided he was safe.

The entry came up. The codes were part of the Koppen climate classification, still used on climate maps today. It had been developed by Wladimir Koppen, a climatologist born in Russia who worked in Germany. Emile said it out loud by accident. "Koppen," he whispered. "Born in Russia, worked in Germany." The kid at the next terminal, a small boy with a dinosaur backpack, looked over.

"You talk to yourself too?"

"Only when something's crucial," Emile said. "This guy made up the letters on climate maps. Every map. He sorted the whole world into codes."

The twist came when he went back for the atlas to double-check the Sahara's code. Priya was already at the atlas shelf, and her notebook was open to a page headed Koppen Classification. She had gotten there first. She had the same fact, the same codes, probably written in neater handwriting. Emile's stomach dropped, because half the value of his discovery had just walked away.

But then he looked at her page again. She had listed the codes, but she had no graphs. She was missing the thing he actually had: the tall rainforest bars and the flat desert line, the percentage of months with almost no rain versus months drowning in it, the temperature lines rising and falling in opposite rhythms. Priya had the name of the system; he had the evidence it described. He sat back down and rebuilt his torn graph on graph paper from the supply drawer, labeling the desert BWh and the rainforest Af in careful block letters.

At closing time he packed his bag, and Priya passed his table on her way out. She glanced at the new graph and stopped.

"You did it by rainfall," she said. "I just did the letters."

"Yeah," Emile said. "You can have the letters." He slid his torn first draft into the recycling bin on his way past the front desk.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: A crescendo means gradually getting louder, and a diminuendo or decrescendo means gradually getting softer.
story:
Charlotte had one week left before the video audition for the youth orchestra, and the last line of her piano piece kept sounding wrong. She played it again in the living room, watching her phone record her on the music stand, and when she listened back she understood why. The ending was supposed to swell and then fade, but her hands jumped straight to loud, like a door slamming instead of a wave.

Her grandfather was in his chair by the window, a frail shape under his gray blanket, listening the way he always did. He used to play trumpet, before his lungs got bad, and he still judged everything. "That was a crescendo and a diminuendo stacked on top of each other," she said, mostly to herself. "That's what the symbols are, right? Gradually getting louder, then gradually getting softer." He nodded once, and she felt her face go warm, because she had known those words for years and still couldn't do them.

She tried counting. If the crescendo spanned four measures, she could give each measure a number, one through four, and make four louder than three, three louder than two. She wrote the numbers in pencil above the notes. The first attempt was lumpy, louder in the wrong spots, and she crossed the numbers out and tried again, spacing them further apart. On the third try the sound rose the way the music asked, a slow climb she could feel in her shoulders.

The diminuendo was harder. Going softer felt like the room was pulling away from her, and twice she hit the final chord so quietly that no sound came out at all, just the thud of felt. "You lost it completely," her grandfather said, and coughed. "A diminuendo means gradually getting softer. There's supposed to be something left at the end."

Charlotte stared at the last chord. Maybe she was thinking about it backward. Instead of subtracting loudness, she could think of it as holding onto something and letting it thin out, like the way the brass in his old recordings went shiny at the edges and then vanished. She played it once more, easing off but keeping her fingers firm, and the final notes hung in the room and faded on their own. Her grandfather's eyes were closed, and he was smiling.

Her mother had authorized her to skip chores all week for practice, one audition for one clean kitchen, but the deal cost her the afternoon she was supposed to help him to his cardiology appointment. He had rescheduled it himself, waving her off, saying the audition mattered more, and she had let him say it.

That night she recorded the final take. The crescendo built, the diminuendo thinned out to almost nothing, and the last chord shimmered there like metal cooling, some quiet alloy of soft and strong. When it ended, she looked at the phone, then at the empty chair by the window, and pressed save.

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: On a river bend, water flows fastest on the outside, eroding that bank, and slowest on the inside, where it deposits sand and gravel.
story:
Hazel pressed her museum badge against the glass case and read the plaque for the third time. Inside the case sat a cross-section model of a canyon, layered rock stacked like a strange cake, and beside it a plastic tub of water, sand, and gravel labeled "Touch Table: Make a River." The contest rules were taped to the wall: explain the canyon model to a judge in under two minutes, and the best explainer won a week at the geology day camp. Hazel wanted that week more than she had wanted anything since the robotics fair, where she had come in second and cried in the supply closet.

Her friend Priya arrived with a notebook and a smug look. "I already figured out my speech," Priya said. "Rain wears the rock down. Easy." She wandered off toward the dinosaur hall, and Hazel stood alone, staring at the tub. Rain wearing rock down would take a very long time, but something bothered her. The model canyon was deep and narrow, not wide and flat like a scraped surface. Something had sliced downward. Something she could not see.

She rolled up her sleeve and tilted the tub so a trickle of water ran across the sand. At first the water went straight. Then she nudged a pebble into its path, and the trickle swerved around it, curving into a bend. She leaned close, chin almost touching the rim.

On the outside of the bend, the sand was collapsing. Little bites of bank slumped into the current and vanished downstream, leaving a steep, undercut edge. On the inside, the water barely seemed to move, and there, right before her eyes, a small crescent of pale sand and gravel was building up, grain by grain, like a tiny beach.

"Fast on that side," she whispered, pointing at the cut bank. "Slow on this side." She turned the tap up, waited, then made herself cease pouring entirely and watch what stayed behind. The steep outer edge kept its shape; the inner crescent kept growing. She scooped a handful of gravel and dropped it upstream. Every piece that reached the bend swept past the outer edge and settled, finally, on the inner curve.

A boy next to her, maybe ten, was watching too. "Why is there a beach there?" he asked.

"Because the water's slowest on the inside of the bend," Hazel said. "Fastest on the outside. That's why this bank gets eaten away and that one gets built up."

She thought about the canyon in the case. A river bending back and forth, cutting deeper on every outside edge, for millions of years. She looked up to find a judge already standing nearby, clipboard in hand, timer indifferent to her racing pulse.

Priya had come back too, and was reading Hazel's wet handprints on the tub's rim. "You're going first," the judge said. "Whenever you're ready."

Hazel took a breath, cupped her hands in the water, and pointed at the sand.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Desert rainfall is not just low but unreliable: a desert may go years with almost no rain and then get a heavy downpour in a single storm.
story:
Asher's flight to Tucson was delayed two hours, which meant his mom had assigned him homework in the middle of Gate B14. "Two graphs," she had said, handing him printed pages before she left for her own gate. "One's a desert, one's a rainforest. Tell me which is which and why." She was a climate scientist and thought even boarding passes were teaching moments.

He spread the pages on the seat beside him. The first graph had tall rainfall bars every single month, steady as teeth on a comb, with temperatures that barely moved. The second graph was strange. Most months showed rainfall bars so short they looked like mistakes, almost nothing, and the temperature line climbed and dropped with the seasons. He pulled out his notebook and wrote, "Graph 1: rainforest. Graph 2: desert." Too easy. His mom would want more.

Across from him sat a girl about his age, hugging a pillow shaped like a frog and blinking hard at the arrivals board. Asher recognized that look. "Is someone landing?" he asked. She nodded. "My grandma. I haven't seen her in a year." Asher dug into his backpack, found the granola bar his mom always packed, and held it out. "For waiting," he said. "Waiting is the worst part."

She took it, and when she saw his graphs she leaned over. "Why does that one look broken?" She pointed at the desert rainfall, where one bar shot up like a tower among all the tiny ones. "That storm dropped more rain in a day than the whole rest of the year," Asher said slowly, tracing the bar with his finger. He stared at it. So the desert wasn't just dry. It was undependable, and then suddenly, violently, not dry at all.

Then he remembered something. Last summer his uncle in Arizona had texted photos of a flooded road, and Asher had asked why a desert town had flood warning signs everywhere. His uncle had written back, "Deserts don't just get little rain, they get wildly unpredictable rain. Some years almost nothing. Then one storm dumps a downpour." At the time Asher had filed it away as a weird grown-up fact. Now he saw it drawn in ink, a single tower in a field of nothing. He copied the idea into his notebook: the desert's problem wasn't only that rainfall was low, it was that you couldn't count on it at all. A rainforest, on the other hand, was so constantly soaked that its plants and animals had evolved to expect it, and clearing those forests could push rare species toward extinction. His mom's articles used that word a lot. He wrote, "Rainforest: reliable. Desert: unreliable. One giant storm can carry a whole year's water." He underlined it twice.

Nearby a screen flashed, and the girl shot to her feet. "That's her flight!" A small woman with a sun hat came down the jetway, and the girl ran and buried her face in her grandma's sweater. Asher watched, then looked back at his notebook. His mom would land in Tucson after him tonight, and he would hold up the page and say, "The desert's rainfall is low AND unreliable, that's the whole answer." Then he took out his phone and texted her one line: "Why does the desert town have flood signs? I figured it out."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: When the brain senses a threat, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing quicker. This is called the fight-or-flight response.
story:
Isaac locked the bathroom door and pressed his palms flat against the sink. His heart was pounding so hard he could feel it in his throat, and when he held up his hands, his fingers trembled like the time he'd carried a full watering can too far. In fifteen minutes he had to walk onto the school stage and play his piano piece, the one he had cherished since his grandmother taught it to him three summers ago. He stared at his shaking hands in the mirror and thought, fever? Flu? He touched his forehead. Cool.

Then he remembered a page from the health curriculum they'd covered in science class back in October. He had barely paid attention then, but one diagram had stuck with him: a brain, two small glands sitting on top of the kidneys, and arrows pointing to a heart and a pair of lungs. When the brain senses a threat, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing quicker. His friend Dex had leaned over and whispered, "It's called the fight-or-flight response," and Mr. Ruiz had made them all repeat it like a chant. Isaac had thought it was boring. Now he stood in the bathroom thinking, I'm not sick. My brain thinks the recital is a threat.

He tested the idea. If adrenaline was causing this, then his fast heart and quick breaths had a distinct pattern: they'd started the moment his name moved up the sign-up list, and they hadn't come with a fever or a sore throat. He exhaled slowly through his mouth, counting to four, then inhaled for four, out for six, the way the science packet had shown. He did it ten times. His shoulders dropped. His hands went still against the porcelain.

That night he decided to test the whole thing properly. He set a bedtime alarm for ten o'clock, put his phone in the kitchen, and read until his eyes got heavy. He did the same thing the next night, and the night after that. By Friday, when he practiced the piece for his teacher, his hands were steady and his breathing came out even. "Whatever you're doing," Ms. Park said, "keep doing it."

On the day of the recital, his heart still sped up as he stood in the wings. But he recognized it now, the whole chain: brain sensing threat, adrenal glands, adrenaline, faster heartbeat, quicker breathing. He wasn't getting sick. His body was getting ready.

He sat down at the piano, took one slow breath, in for four, out for six, and placed his fingers on the opening chord.

"Play it like it's just us in the kitchen," his grandmother had said once. He smiled, and began.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: In improv, an offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, such as a place, a name or a problem.
story:
On the first morning of drama camp, Payton's group sat in a circle on the gym floor, and the counselor, Rex, said they would learn improv. "You and a partner make up a scene on the spot," he said. "Rules come later. Let's just try it." Payton bounced on her knees. She wanted the fun part, the acting, not the rules part.

Her partner was a quiet kid named Marco. Rex clapped his hands and told them to start, so Payton said, "Grandma, the spaceship is leaking!" Marco stared at the floor, then said, "No, it isn't. There's no spaceship." The scene collapsed like a dropped tent. Rex just said, "Switch it up," and Marco mimed holding a long stick, swinging it back and forth over an imaginary lake.

Payton froze. What was she supposed to do with a stick? Then she noticed the swing of it, the patient rhythm, the way Marco kept his eyes on some invisible point in the water. He wasn't just waving his arms. He was telling her something: we're at a lake, we're fishing, there's probably a problem coming. It was like a signal hidden inside his movements, and once she caught it, she couldn't unsee it. Every word and gesture was handing her information about the scene, and if she ignored the information, the scene starved. The gym around them was sparse, just a circle of kids and an empty floor, and yet Marco had just built a whole lake out of one invisible rod.

She stepped in fast. "Dad, you've been out here for hours and the fish aren't biting." Marco's face lit up. "They're all hiding," he said, "since the thing fell in the lake last night." Now he was handing her a problem, a good one, and she grabbed it. "You mean the meteor?" Marco laughed and reeled in an imaginary fish so heavy he staggered backward into the circle.

Afterward, breathless, Payton told Rex about the fishing rod. "I almost missed it," she said. "But everything he did was an offer." Rex nodded, and Payton spun back to Marco, already planning. "Same partners tomorrow? I want to see what you drop in the lake next."

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: A blues in the key of A is usually played with the chords A7, D7 and E7, which are dominant seventh chords.
story:
Luca stood in the wings of the concert hall with his guitar strap cutting into his shoulder, watching the stage crew tape down cables. In twenty minutes he was supposed to join Ms. Ruiz's small combo for one song at the student showcase, and the song had no written solo. "You improvise," Ms. Ruiz had said, waving her hand like it was the easiest thing in the world. "Blues in A. Twelve bars. You'll be fine." Luca did not feel fine.

The pianist, a tall ninth grader named Simone, was already on stage testing the bench height. Luca crossed over, the floorboards humming faintly under the audience murmur that had started to circulate through the hall like a slow tide. "Okay," Luca said, keeping his voice low, "twelve bars. What chords?" Simone frowned. "It's a blues. In A." "I know that part. But which chords?" Simone spread her hands over the keys without playing them, thinking. "A blues in A is usually played with the chords A7, D7 and E7. They're dominant seventh chords." Luca nodded as if this settled everything, though his stomach was doing a slow flip. He only knew two shapes on the guitar for dominant sevenths, and one of them, he suspected, was wrong.

Backstage, he found a quiet corner behind a rack of velvet curtains that smelled like dust and old perfume. He formed the A7 shape and strummed it softly. It sounded right, warm and slightly crooked, like a blues chord should. Then he made his other shape, the one his cousin had shown him last summer, and moved it to the fifth fret. He played it alongside a recording hummed under his breath. Wrong. Completely, obviously wrong. So that was it. His cousin had taught him a major shape and called it a seventh, and Luca had believed him for months. It was like discovering a supposed artisan had been gluing his handmade chairs together with tape. He laughed once, sharp and surprised, and a stagehand glanced over.

There was no time to feel embarrassed. Ms. Ruiz was beckoning from the wings, the lights had gone amber, and Luca walked out into the smell of hot spotlights and rosin. The drummer counted four. Simone's left hand landed on A7, and Luca, no longer guessing, bent his third string up and let the note wail.

"Nice," Simone whispered between bars, grinning.

"That was a legitimate seventh," Luca whispered back, and took the solo straight into the turnaround.

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: A pivot table's summary can be switched from Sum or Count to Average, turning a column of one-to-five ratings into the mean rating for each grade.
story:
Hazel had promised the student council she would have the field trip survey results ready by Monday, and now it was Sunday afternoon at Priya's house, with the spreadsheet open and a deadline hanging over her like an ominous cloud. Two hundred students had rated the museum trip from one to five, and Miss Okafor wanted to know which grade had liked it best. The numbers sat in one long column, and Hazel had no idea how to make them say anything.

"Watch this," Priya said, pulling the laptop toward her. Priya's secret ambition was to be the youngest person ever hired at her brother's tech company, and she collected spreadsheet tricks the way other kids collected stickers. She clicked through the menus, dragged the grade column into one box and the rating column into another, and suddenly the two hundred answers folded themselves into four tidy rows: one per grade, each with a single number beside it.

"Those are counts," Priya said. "How many kids from each grade answered. Useful, but not what you need."

Hazel frowned at the screen. The sixth grade had returned forty-two surveys, the seventh grade only thirty-one, so the counts couldn't tell her who liked the trip more. A bigger number just meant more kids. She clicked on the summary box, half guessing, and a small menu dropped down: Sum, Count, Average. She remembered averaging her quiz scores once, adding them up and dividing. She chose Average, and the numbers changed. Now each grade had a rating between one and five, the mean of every answer in that grade. Sixth grade showed 3.2. Seventh grade showed 4.6.

"Wait, do that again," Hazel said, afraid it would vanish. She switched back to Count, then to Average again, watching the same column of answers become two completely different things. "So the seventh grade actually liked it more. Even though fewer of them went."

Priya leaned back with her arms crossed, clearly hoping for praise, and Hazel felt a stab of envy at how easily the whole thing had come to her. But Hazel was the one on student council, and she was the one who had found the Average setting. She copied the four numbers into her notes, then sat looking at the 4.6.

"Something's wrong," Priya said, peering closer. "The eighth grade says 5.0. Every single eighth grader gave it a five?" That seemed too neat, and Hazel had a suspicion she couldn't see directly, only test. She sorted the raw sheet by grade and scrolled. There, in a block of twelve rows, sat an identical stack of fives, all submitted within the same two minutes, from names like "Cool Kid" and "Definitely Real Student."

"Someone stuffed the ballot box," Hazel said. Priya was already reaching for the laptop. "Delete them?"

"No. Leave them. I want the council to see it themselves." Hazel saved the file and started a new email to Miss Okafor, typing the subject line: "Survey results, plus a problem."
